title: Odyssey - Book I, The Council of the Gods
author: Homer
description: The opening of Homer's Odyssey, introducing Odysseus and his long journey home from Troy.

sections.greek:
Ἄνδρα μοι ἔννεπε, Μοῦσα, πολύτροπον, ὃς μάλα πολλὰ
πλάγχθη, ἐπεὶ Τροίης ἱερὸν πτολίεθρον ἔπερσε·
πολλῶν δ᾽ ἀνθρώπων ἴδεν ἄστεα καὶ νόον ἔγνω,
πολλὰ δ᾽ ὅ γ᾽ ἐν πόντῳ πάθεν ἄλγεα ὃν κατὰ θυμόν,
ἀρνύμενος ἥν τε ψυχὴν καὶ νόστον ἑταίρων.
ἀλλ᾽ οὐδ᾽ ὣς ἑτάρους ἐρρύσατο, ἱέμενός περ·
αὐτῶν γὰρ σφετέρῃσιν ἀτασθαλίῃσιν ὄλοντο,
νήπιοι, οἳ κατὰ βοῦς Ὑπερίονος Ἠελίοιο
ἤσθιον· αὐτὰρ ὁ τοῖσιν ἀφείλετο νόστιμον ἦμαρ.
τῶν ἁμόθεν γε, θεά, θύγατερ Διός, εἰπὲ καὶ ἡμῖν.
sections.translation: Tell me, Muse, of the man of many ways, who wandered far and wide after he sacked the sacred citadel of Troy. Many were the men whose cities he saw and whose minds he learned, and many the pains he suffered in his heart upon the sea, striving to save his own life and the homecoming of his companions. But even so he could not save his companions, eager though he was, for they perished through their own blind folly, the fools, who devoured the cattle of Helios Hyperion; and he took from them the day of their return. Of these things, goddess, daughter of Zeus, beginning from somewhere, tell us also.

lineByLine.greek: Ἄνδρα μοι ἔννεπε, Μοῦσα, πολύτροπον, ὃς μάλα πολλὰ
lineByLine.transliteration: Andra moi ennepe, Mousa, polytropon, hos mala polla
lineByLine.translation: Tell me, Muse, of the man of many turns, who very much
lineByLine.notes: ἄνδρα: echoes Virgil's virum; πολύτροπον: 'of many turns' - cunning, versatile

lineByLine.greek: πλάγχθη, ἐπεὶ Τροίης ἱερὸν πτολίεθρον ἔπερσε·
lineByLine.transliteration: planchthē, epei Troiēs hieron ptoliethron eperse
lineByLine.translation: wandered, after he sacked the sacred citadel of Troy
lineByLine.notes: πτολίεθρον: poetic form of πόλις; ἔπερσε: aorist of πέρθω, 'sack'

lineByLine.greek: πολλῶν δ᾽ ἀνθρώπων ἴδεν ἄστεα καὶ νόον ἔγνω
lineByLine.transliteration: pollōn d' anthrōpōn iden astea kai noon egnō
lineByLine.translation: and saw the cities of many men and knew their mind
lineByLine.notes: νόον ἔγνω: 'knew their mind' - Odysseus learns from experience

lineByLine.greek: πολλὰ δ᾽ ὅ γ᾽ ἐν πόντῳ πάθεν ἄλγεα ὃν κατὰ θυμόν
lineByLine.transliteration: polla d' ho g' en pontō pathen algea hon kata thymon
lineByLine.translation: and many pains he suffered on the sea in his heart
lineByLine.notes: πόντος: the sea (especially open sea); θυμός: heart, spirit

lineByLine.greek: ἀρνύμενος ἥν τε ψυχὴν καὶ νόστον ἑταίρων
lineByLine.transliteration: arnymenos hēn te psychēn kai noston hetairōn
lineByLine.translation: striving to win his own life and the homecoming of his companions
lineByLine.notes: νόστος: homecoming - the central theme of the poem

lineByLine.greek: ἀλλ᾽ οὐδ᾽ ὣς ἑτάρους ἐρρύσατο, ἱέμενός περ·
lineByLine.transliteration: all' oud' hōs hetarous errysato, hiemenos per
lineByLine.translation: but even so he could not save his companions, eager though he was
for they perished through their own blind folly
lineByLine.notes: ἀτασθαλίαι: reckless folly - the companions' tragic flaw

lineByLine.greek: νήπιοι, οἳ κατὰ βοῦς Ὑπερίονος Ἠελίοιο
lineByLine.transliteration: nēpioi, hoi kata bous Hyperionos Hēelioio
lineByLine.translation: fools, who the cattle of Helios Hyperion
lineByLine.notes: νήπιοι: 'fools, children' - moral judgment on the crew

lineByLine.greek: ἤσθιον· αὐτὰρ ὁ τοῖσιν ἀφείλετο νόστιμον ἦμαρ
lineByLine.transliteration: ēsthion; autar ho toisin apheileto nostimon hēmar
lineByLine.translation: devoured; but he [Helios] took from them the day of return
lineByLine.notes: νόστιμον ἦμαρ: 'day of homecoming' - death is loss of return

lineByLine.greek: τῶν ἁμόθεν γε, θεά, θύγατερ Διός, εἰπὲ καὶ ἡμῖν
lineByLine.transliteration: tōn hamothen ge, thea, thygater Dios, eipe kai hēmin
lineByLine.translation: Of these things, from some point, goddess, daughter of Zeus, tell us also
lineByLine.notes: ἁμόθεν: 'from somewhere' - poet invites Muse to begin where she wishes

historicalContext: The Odyssey, Homer's second epic, tells of Odysseus's ten-year journey home from Troy. It explores themes of homecoming, identity, and the tension between adventure and domestic life.
literaryFeatures: Focus on a single hero (ἄνδρα) vs. the Iliad's focus on wrath
πολύτροπος captures Odysseus's defining quality: cunning adaptability
Foreshadowing of the crew's fate in the proem
Contrast between hero who survives and companions who perish
